title: Architecture review - KV cache eviction policy notes
content:
Meeting: Architecture review — KV cache eviction policy
Date: 2026-03-15
Time: 10:00–11:00 PT
Location: Zoom / #eng-serving-runtime-arch
Facilitator: Aisha Patel
Note-taker: Liam Chen

Purpose:
Review RFC options for KV cache eviction (LRU variants, TTL, size/weight-based policies) and decide on a primary policy for the next rollout. Ensure compatibility with existing sharding and routing changes from RFC-142.

Attendees:
- Aisha Patel (owner)
- Liam Chen
- Sofia Martinez
- Noah Williams
- Priya Singh
- Ravi Kapoor
- (joined late) Marcus Li

Summary / TL;DR:
Agreed to adopt a hybrid eviction policy: segmented LRU (hot/cold) as the primary mechanism, augmented with per-entry TTL and a size-weighted eviction cap per model shard. This balances latency for hot keys, prevents unbounded memory growth, and keeps predictable unit economics. We will implement as an opt-in feature behind a feature flag for 2 weeks of canary traffic before broad rollout.

Discussion notes (detailed):
1) Problem framing
- Current cache uses simple LRU with global capacity. Several issues surfaced in load tests and production canaries: long-tail hot keys displacing useful prefixes, memory spikes on large batches, and uneven per-tenant model cache pressure.
- Requirement: low tail latency for hot prefixes, bounded memory per shard, predictable eviction behavior for multi-tenant workloads.

2) Candidate designs reviewed
A. Plain LRU (current): simple, low overhead, but poor behavior with skewed access patterns.
B. Segmented LRU (SLRU): split into hot/cold segments; new/rare entries go to cold; promoted to hot on repeated access. Improves retention for hot keys.
C. TTL + LRU: entries have time-to-live; combined with LRU helps clear stale cached prefixes for long-tail models.
D. Weight/size-based eviction: make eviction decisions based on entry size (tokens, kv-length) to prevent large entries from crowding the cache.
E. Per-model quotas: enforce per-model cache caps to ensure noisy neighbors don't evict other tenants' hot keys.

3) Tradeoffs discussed
- SLRU adds modest bookkeeping (per-segment counters) and is good for hot-key retention; complexity is manageable in the runtime.
- TTL needs careful defaults; too short reduces hit rate, too long leads to stale state. TTL should be configurable per-model/route and default to a conservative value (e.g., 30m) with an override API.
- Weight-based eviction increases cpu on eviction decisions but is necessary for mixed entry sizes (e.g., long-context models). Implementation can approximate weights to reduce overhead.
- Per-model quotas are operationally important for multi-tenant Dedicated deployments; for hosted API, quotas should be configurable per-customer plan.

4) Compatibility with sharding & routing (RFC-142)
- Sharding is (by key hash) across nodes; eviction policy must be local to shard. We must ensure the per-model quota maps to (model, shard) so that cross-shard leak doesn't occur. Proposal: compute per-model global cap and translate to per-shard cap by proportional split based on shard capacity (static evenly split for initial rollout).
- Routing decisions that fall back to compatible model variants must clear/refresh cache usage metrics so fallback doesn't spuriously inflate hot counts.

5) Performance & telemetry concerns
- Benchmarks requested: end-to-end 95/99p latency with SLRU vs LRU under realistic key skew; memory overhead for SLRU bookkeeping; CPU overhead for weight computation.
- Telemetry to add: per-shard cache hit/miss, promotion rate (cold->hot), eviction reasons (size, ttl, quota), per-model cache utilization, and correlation with tail latency spikes.

6) Rollout plan
- Phase 0 (dev): implement SLRU + optional TTL + weight-aware pruning behind feature flag. Add config knobs via route/model config file.
- Phase 1 (canary): enable for 5% serving traffic on a small set of stable models (internal customers + synthetic load) for 2 weeks. Collect telemetry and run regression evals using Redwood Optimize prompt sets.
- Phase 2 (dedicated opt-in): expose per-model quota controls in Dedicated config UI; allow platform teams to opt in.
- Phase 3 (full rollout): enable for hosted API default for models with long context windows after no regressions found.

7) Open questions / unresolved items
- Exact default TTL value: proposal 30 minutes for hosted, 60 minutes for Dedicated; action: run hit-rate sensitivity experiment (see action items).
- Weight approximation algorithm: exact weight = sum(token_count * per-entry-factor) vs approximate bucketing; action: prototype both and measure CPU overhead.
- Per-shard quota split: static even split vs dynamic proportional to active connections; action: start with even split, evaluate later.
- What to do for function-calling/tool outputs that have large kv entries: treat as high-weight entries and consider bypass cache for ephemeral tool outputs.

8) Decisions made
- Adopt segmented LRU as primary eviction policy (SLRU).
- Add per-entry TTL, configurable per-route/model; default to 30m for initial experiments.
- Implement size-weighted eviction as an approximation (bucketed weights) to limit overhead.
- Enforce per-model cache caps, translated to per-shard even splits for rollout.
- Feature-gate behind runtime flag and rollout via canary.

9) Action items (owner - due):
- Implement SLRU skeleton + hot/cold counters in serving runtime (Ravi Kapoor) - due 2026-03-29
- Prototype weight approximation and measure CPU overhead (Noah Williams) - due 2026-03-22
- Run TTL sensitivity experiments on canary models to pick defaults (Sofia Martinez) - due 2026-03-24
- Add telemetry metrics (hit/miss, promotion rate, eviction reason) and dashboard (Priya Singh) - due 2026-03-26
- Update RFC doc to reflect final decision and architecture diagrams (Aisha Patel) - due 2026-03-20
- Create canary config and rollout playbook (Liam Chen) - due 2026-03-28

Appendix: Notes from debate
- Marcus raised concern about memory fragmentation with mixed-size entries; consensus to prefer weight-based pruning to avoid repeated full-cache compaction.
- Priya emphasized observability: we must be able to attribute tail-latency regression to cache policy changes quickly — therefore detailed eviction_reason telemetry is required before canary.
- Ravi suggested a fallback mechanism: if canary induces tail regression, automatically revert to previous policy per-route with an API call and rollout flag. Agreed to include in playbook.

References:
- KV Cache Sharding RFC (RFC-142): https://confluence.redwood.com/display/INF/KV-Cache-Sharding-RFC-142
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/678
- Jira: INF-2345 (kv-cache-eviction-policy)

Next meeting: follow-up sync to review prototypes and TTL experiment results — tentatively 2026-03-23 10:00 PT.
